title: Supreme Court to render its decision on Quebec's secularism law today

image.caption: The grand hall of the temporary Supreme Court of Canada, located in the West Memorial Building in Ottawa is hosting, by far, the largest lockup in its history as journalists and legal teams await the top court's ruling on Bill 21. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

On Friday morning, a record number of journalists and lawyers of record who've been sworn to confidentiality will be the first to read a historic judgment from the Supreme Court of Canada determining the fate of Quebec's controversial Bill 21.
Judgment addressing the challenge to Bill 21 will be released at 9:45 a.m. ET

On Friday morning, journalists and lawyers of record who've been sworn to confidentiality will be the first to read a historic judgment from the Supreme Court of Canada determining the fate of Quebec's controversial Bill 21.
The 90-minute lockup will be the biggest in the top court's history, hosting legal teams for 51 individuals, groups and governments from across the country, including six auditors general.
All those eyes will pore over a judgment that could overturn Bill 21, Quebec's secularism law preventing some public-sector workers from wearing religious symbols while on the job.
The court could also rein in the use of the notwithstanding clause, which allows provinces and the federal government to override some Charter rights for five-year renewable increments.
It could also do neither of these things — simply uphold the law in its current form and leave issues around the notwithstanding clause alone.
No matter what the outcome, however, the judgment will be historic.

items: What's at stake as Canada's top court ruling on Quebec secularism law looms
6 key moments from the Supreme Court challenge of Quebec's secularism law

blocks.text: Bill 21, the Act respecting the laicity of the State, became law on June 19, 2019.
It prohibits the wearing of religious symbols including but not limited to hijabs, turbans, yarmulkes, crucifixes and Sikh kirpans by some public service workers while they're on the job.

When the law was first passed, it specifically impacted educators like teachers and principals, police officers, government lawyers and even members of the province's legislature, including Quebec's minister of justice and the Speaker of the National Assembly.
Groups challenging Quebec secularism law in Supreme Court say it breaches basic rights
The law also required these public-sector workers to do their jobs with their faces uncovered unless they need it covered for non-religious reasons such as a health issue or disability.
For security or identity verification reasons, people can be denied access to public services unless they also have their faces uncovered.
Bill 21 has resulted in job losses across the province as people change professions or move to other parts of the country to escape the law.
Overriding Charter protections

All of those provisions violated civil liberty protections in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, but Bill 21 became law anyway because both charters have an override clause.

The notwithstanding clause, Section 33 of the federal Charter, can override certain sections — including Section 2 and sections 7 to 15, which deal with fundamental freedoms, legal rights and equality rights.
Once invoked, Section 33 prevents any judicial review of the legislation in question. After five years, the clause ceases to have any effect — unless it is re-enacted.

Bill 21 also invoked the Quebec Charter's version of the notwithstanding clause, Section 52, which allows rights from Section 1 to Section 38 to be overridden until the National Assembly in Quebec repeals the law.
Challenging Bill 21

In April of 2021 the Quebec Superior Court ruled on a constitutional challenge to Bill 21, largely upholding the law while at the same time finding some constitutional rights had been improperly overridden.

The court said Bill 21 improperly violated Section 3 of the federal Charter by interfering with protected democratic rights because it would prevent people from serving in elected office. The law remained in effect but could not apply to members of the Quebec legislature.

The court also ruled that Bill 21 violated minority language education rights guaranteed by Section 23 of the federal Charter — which includes the management and control over minority language institutions.

In early 2024 the Quebec Court of Appeal mostly upheld the lower court's decision but it tossed out the section on minority language rights, saying it did not impact the content of what was taught, only who was hired to teach it.
Top court has its say
Seven justices of the Supreme Court of Canada heard the case over four days in March, which the court says was one of the longest-ever hearings for a case at Canada's top court.
Over those four days it was asked to weigh in on a number of questions including:

items: Whether the notwithstanding clause was properly used.
Whether there are limits on use of the clause.
Whether a court can issue a non-binding declaration saying that while the law stands — because of the notwithstanding clause — it still violates certain rights.
Whether the federal Charter's guarantee of equal rights for both males and females in Section 28 has been violated by Bill 21.
Whether Bill 21 infringes on English-language education rights under Section 23 of the federal Charter.
Whether the face-uncovering requirement for National Assembly members violated democratic rights in Section 3 of the Charter.
Whether Bill 21 is consistent with certain pre-Confederation laws.

blocks.text: The Supreme Court can pick and choose which of these questions it decides need settling. It can also refer one or more questions back to lower courts with guidance on how to proceed.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.
